exam: What immediate step should you take when a patient develops acute dyspnoea during a transfusion? — Stop the transfusion and assess airway, breathing, and circulation.
How do you differentiate TRALI from TACO at the bedside? — Look for signs of fluid overload (elevated JVP, peripheral oedema) and use BNP; TRALI has normal volume status.
A patient on plasma transfusion becomes hypoxic with bilateral infiltrates but normal cardiac exam. What is the most likely diagnosis? — TRALI, because of non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
Why are male‑only plasma donors preferred in many blood banks? — They have a lower prevalence of anti‑HLA antibodies, reducing TRALI risk.
What ventilatory strategy is recommended for severe TRALI? — Lung‑protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) and adequate PEEP.
If antibody testing is unavailable, how should you manage a suspected TRALI case? — Treat as TRALI clinically: stop transfusion, provide oxygen/ventilatory support, and document the reaction.
What are the red‑flag laboratory values indicating severe TRALI? — PaO₂/FiO₂ <100 mmHg, rising lactate, and worsening acidosis.
Explain why corticosteroids are not routinely used in TRALI. — Evidence does not show benefit; they may increase infection risk and mask other causes.
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: TRALI is a non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema caused by donor anti‑leukocyte antibodies activating recipient neutrophils, leading to capillary leak. It presents rapidly after transfusion and is a leading cause of transfusion‑related mortality, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Onset ≤6 h after transfusion
PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤300 mmHg or SpO₂ < 90 % on room air
New bilateral infiltrates on chest X‑ray
Absence of left‑sided heart failure signs
sections.p: TRALI is an acute respiratory distress syndrome that occurs within 6 hours of a blood product transfusion, characterized by hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, and no evidence of circulatory overload.

b: Mild: PaO₂/FiO₂ 200–300 mmHg
Moderate: PaO₂/FiO₂ 100–200 mmHg
Severe: PaO₂/FiO₂ <100 mmHg
sections.p: Severity follows the Berlin ARDS criteria, applied to the transfusion context.

b: Donor anti‑HLA class I/II antibodies (most common)
Donor anti‑HNA antibodies
Two‑hit model: recipient inflammation (infection, surgery) + donor antibodies
Stored plasma products with bioactive lipids
sections.p: TRALI is immune‑mediated in most cases; a minority are due to biologically active lipids in stored blood.

b: Rapid onset (minutes‑hours) after transfusion
Tachypnoea >30 breaths/min
SpO₂ < 90 % on room air
Bilateral basal crackles
sections.p: Patients develop sudden dyspnoea, cough, tachypnoea, and hypoxaemia, often with fever and a non‑productive cough. Auscultation shows diffuse crackles without a clear cardiac murmur.
Focus on confirming non‑cardiogenic edema, ruling out cardiac failure, and identifying the antibody source.

t.b: Does the patient have bilateral infiltrates? → Positive supports TRALI; normal film argues against.
What is the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio? → ≤300 mmHg confirms acute lung injury; guides severity.
Is there cardiac overload? → Low levels favour TRALI; high levels suggest cardiogenic edema.
Is a donor antibody present? → Positive confirms immune TRALI; negative points to non‑immune cause.

b: Rapid fall in SpO₂ despite oxygen
PaO₂/FiO₂ <100 mmHg
Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors
Development of secondary infection
sections.p: Early recognition prevents progression to severe ARDS and multi‑organ failure.

b: Cease all blood products; consider returning the implicated unit for investigation
Give supplemental oxygen; consider high‑flow nasal cannula or CPAP if needed
If severe, intubate with lung‑protective ventilation (tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O)
Avoid diuretics unless clear volume overload; TRALI is not fluid overload
Consider corticosteroids only in refractory cases, not routine
sections.p: Stop the transfusion immediately, provide supportive care, and treat the underlying cause of the first hit.

b: Repeat chest imaging 24 h after resolution
Document the reaction in the transfusion service database
Prefer male‑only plasma donors to reduce anti‑HLA antibody exposure
Use pathogen‑reduced plasma where available
sections.p: Monitor respiratory status for 24‑48 h; educate staff on donor screening.

b: Transfusion‑associated circulatory overload (TACO) – cardiac‑related, responds to diuretics
Anaphylactic transfusion reaction – bronchospasm, urticaria, hypotension
Septic transfusion reaction – fever, rigors, positive blood cultures
sections.p: Conditions that cause acute respiratory distress after transfusion.

b: Normal BNP does not completely exclude cardiac contribution in mixed pathology
Mildly elevated BNP can be seen in sepsis, misleading toward TACO
Chest X‑ray may be normal early; ultrasound is more sensitive
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
